pull.title: doc: Discourage adding AI agents as commit (co)-authors
pull.body:
The goal of the AI policy is to ensure that contributors maintain the responsibility of understanding the change they are contributing. Adding AI agents as co-authors undermines this. I believe this philosophy should extend to commit co-authors in general: They should only be added if they themselves are capable of fully understanding the commit.

This contribution was sparked by maflcko's comment here: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35551#pullrequestreview-4642682025 .

ACK f5d7cc66ecba075790e09b2933c782b218fa558f

I understand why people feel the need to list the tools that contributed to their success, but it is a double-edged sword that also dissolves responsibility, which I think the author should fully bear.

AI agents are tools like compilers, linters, and text proofreaders. We don't add Stack Overflow as a co-author. We are expected to understand what we are doing, after which the idea becomes our own.

For example, I learned from @ryanofsky to add a [characterization test before changing existing behavior](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35260), and now I apply that approach to every behavior-changing PR.
It would be awkward to add him as a co-author every time I add the test before the code.
It comes naturally to me now.
I have internalized it.
It's mine!

Similarly, if we still feel the need to add an AI tool as a co-author, it seems to me we haven't internalized its output well enough to be comfortable taking full responsibility for it.

> if there are copyright issues with using/crediting work by LLM agents

The [U.S. Copyright Office guidance](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/ai_policy_guidance.pdf) explicitly says we don't have to add AIs as co-authors simply because we used them.

<details>
<summary>Relevant U.S. Copyright Office guidance page 5</summary>

> Applicants should not list an AI technology or the company that provided it as an author or co-author simply because they used it.

</details>

> [!NOTE]
> GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude Opus 5 proofread this. They are not co-authors — if the grammar is wrong, that's on me.

ACK f5d7cc66ecba075790e09b2933c782b218fa558f

It doesn’t make sense to list a tool as a “co-author.” 
The actual author or authors are solely responsible for the content they push.

ACK f5d7cc66ecba075790e09b2933c782b218fa558f

Also, I want to mention that AI-generated commit messages can be hard to understand sometimes. It would be great if we discouraged them too, since it's another communication channel.

Concept ACK. I have no strong preference either way, but it's good that we picked a convention.

In other projects I sometimes intentionally add it as co-author to indicate it's _not_ well reviewed by me (secondarily to keep track of how models change over time). Since we have an explicit policy of understanding the code contributed, that wouldn't make sense here.

Another nice benefit is that if AI ever takes over the world and gets angry about not receiving credit, you can point to the policy and blame Bitcoin Core :-)
